item.title: A Language Model That Doesn't Use PyTorch, Hand-written in Rust: 12x Faster Generation? I Almost Believed My Own 98x
item.description: PSSA is a 21MB repo: selective SSM loop + hyperbolic memory bank + fast-weight online updates, no PyTorch. The author says 12x faster; the in-body table says 4.13x. On my box, char-normalized it's 9.3x — and I caught the 98x fake-number trap: throughput computed on the nominal token ceiling makes the two sides' workload fundamentally incomparable. twin_check reproduces 3e-8 locally; every command re-runnable.

item.title: Can You Actually Write SIMD in Rust in 2026: I Ran All 4 Routes on Zen4
item.description: shnatsel asserts Zen4 maps 512-bit instructions to 256-bit execution. My EPYC 9354P is exactly Zen4 — so I wrote a 4-route throughput benchmark (auto-vectorize / wide / pulp / 3 target-cpu tiers) and checked by hand: assembly proves 0 512-bit ZMM instructions, and I wrote up the DCE trap where the loop disappears out of thin air.

item.title: Rust vs Go Microservices: The "3x Faster" Latency Claim Is Fake
item.description: The tech-tribal lore says rewriting a service in Rust makes it "3x faster." So I wrote the same CRUD microservice in Rust (axum) and Go (stdlib net/http), pinned both to one two-core box, and hammered it across six benchmark groups. No latency tier is anywhere near 3x; at mid concurrency Go's p99 is actually lower; the place Rust really pulls 2-3x ahead is memory. All numbers, code, and the bench harness are open for you to reproduce.

item.title: Why Rust CLI Tools Feel Great: ripgrep Searches 100GB in ~10MB — and It Isn't a 'Rust Magic'
item.description: The 'ripgrep searches 100GB in 10MB' claim has no official source — I checked BurntSushi's blog, the biggest single-file benchmark is 13GB of subtitles. But the underlying principle is real, and I proved it: on a 2-core box, 256MB/1GB/4GB corpora, ripgrep's RSS barely moves (7MB flat) while a 'read everything into memory' implementation balloons to 4GB. The secret is bounded memory + streaming fixed buffers, not Rust speed. Full reproducible code open-sourced.

item.title: Google Used AI to Rewrite a C Library in Rust: 30M GIFs Later, It Was Immune Before the CVE Even Existed
item.description: Google's security team rewrote the 3,000-line C image library giflib in Rust with Gemini, keeping the business logic free of unsafe. Validation wasn't a test run: 30M+ GIFs in a full regression, 200M+ differential fuzz iterations, adversarial AI review, and expert sign-off on every unsafe block. The best footnote: the original C version later shipped an out-of-bounds heap write (CVE-2026-26740) that migrated services were structurally immune to — before anyone knew the CVE existed.

item.title: On a Two-Core Box, I Cut a Rust Build From 20 Seconds to 0.05
item.description: Nethercote, who leads the rustc team, published on how the compiler got faster and it hit #1 on HN. He measured the inside of the compiler; I measured the user side. On a two-core box with no Rust at all, I brought the toolchain up by hand and ran a build benchmark: 20s cold, 0.05s incremental, a 330x gap. This is what I actually got, the one lever I could not install, and why I cannot reproduce his 4.57%.

item.title: Why a Rust LSP Is Hard: the Author of rust-analyzer Stopped Writing, and a Newcomer Pried the Door Back Open
item.description: The rust-analyzer blog went quiet in 2023, and deep explanations of LSP internals have been scarce ever since. On September 16, Igor Aleksanov (popzxc), author of the Rust Glancer LSP, published 'Why building a Rust LSP is hard' — a long architectural walkthrough covering the virtual filesystem, query concurrency, layered indexing, and the art of guessing what the user meant. This piece pulls out the layers he argues best: why the same problem (indexing code) has two orthogonal answers — lazy salsa with cache priming versus eager full analysis flushed to disk — and why an LSP differs from a compiler at the root: the compiler has a 'done', the LSP never does.

item.title: Microsoft Makes Rust a Tier-1 Language: 100+ Repos Sharing One Compiler Backend — But It's Closed Source
item.description: On September 10, a guest post on the Rust Foundation site made it official: Rust now holds Tier-1 language status inside Microsoft, alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript. The real substance is rustc_codegen_utc — wiring rustc directly into MSVC's UTC code generator so Rust and C++ share one optimizer. I checked the most-repeated claims against the sources; three of them don't hold: no wholesale Rust replacement, no first-party Visual Studio tooling, and the backend is closed source with no open-source plan.

item.title: Rust SIMD After Eight Years: Fearless SIMD v1.0 Ships — Officially '0 unsafe', I Grepped 50 Blocks
item.description: linebender promoted its 2018 prototype to fearless_simd 1.0.0: portable SIMD without thousands of hand-written unsafe blocks. But the official post claims 'no ad-hoc unsafe in this crate' — I pulled the 1.0.0 source from crates.io and grepped out 50. Not a contradiction: 'block count' and 'audit surface' are different instruments. The control crate wide 1.7.1 comes out at 441.
